solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mark's son having game with mother

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
tig is the playground chasing game also called tag
an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A boy called Mark is off playing a game with his mum.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as a possessive but is the link 'has'. Tig, a playground chasing game, is the British name for tag.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of disgrace, or more literally a visible spot or brand on the body.

clue.text: Redundant old male, in a sense

indicators.note: placing one thing within another means the second wraps around the first

parts.note: one of the five senses
O is the usual abbreviation for old
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: An elderly man laid off from work is redundant, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redundant old male' paints a man made jobless, but the definition is only 'Redundant' in its sense of superfluous.
explanation.definitionFit: Something redundant is surplus to requirements, more than is needed, which is an excess.

clue.text: Good novel, their worst author

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good

indicators.note: novel means new and original, so the letters take a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A reviewer's backhanded verdict: a good book, though by their weakest writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like the noun being praised, but it is the adjective signalling rearrangement of the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghostwriter is someone hired to write books credited to another person, still a kind of writer.

clue.text: Score using both legs

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a total, the sum of points or goals

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for the combined result, as in 'on aggregate'
definitions.meaning: second meaning, cryptically put: combined across the home and away matches of a two-leg cup tie

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a goal struck with both feet; in football knockout ties played over two matches, or legs, the winner is decided by the combined score.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is a sum total, and as an adjective it describes a result combined from both matches of a tie.

clue.text: Some pseudonym as the adopted title?

indicators.note: taking only some of the text means a run of letters sits inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the next three

explanation.surface: Asks whether a writer's chosen pen name serves as the title they adopt.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through pseudonyM AS THE ADopted; 'the' does double duty in the surface and the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: A masthead is the newspaper's name printed in large type across the top of its front page.

clue.text: Bringing up a child causes …

parts.note: surface reading: raising a youngster, which the ellipsis suggests leads to poverty
setter's reading: vomiting, caused by carrying a baby in early pregnancy

explanation.surface: Raising a child causes poverty, the trailing dots carrying on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to the next clue so the two read as one sentence, but each clue is solved separately. 'Bringing up' means throwing up.
explanation.definitionFit: Nausea and vomiting are common in early pregnancy, the symptoms caused by an expected baby.

clue.text: … poor family to be thrown into street

indicators.note: something thrown into a place ends up inside it, enclosed by it

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
one's kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: A poor family is evicted onto the street, continuing the hardship of the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Skint is British slang for having no money.
explanation.definitionFit: Skint is informal British slang for broke, having no money at all.

clue.text: What is acceptable in hotels

indicators.note: being within something means sitting surrounded by it

parts.note: H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet; the plural gives two
U means upper-class, hence socially acceptable

explanation.surface: Asks what counts as proper behaviour in hotels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What is' reads as a question opener, but 'What' alone is the definition, as an exclamation of puzzlement. U for upper-class comes from the old debate on 'U and non-U' usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of confusion or surprise when someone fails to understand what was said.

clue.text: Too controlled to be a failure

parts.note: too in its sense of as well
to run a business is to control it

explanation.surface: Someone so rigid and restrained that they are doomed to fail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too controlled' reads as overly restrained, but splits into a word for 'as well' and a past tense of 'managed'.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse that finishes out of the places, hence any unsuccessful or undistinguished person.

clue.text: Departed from our English town (Barking)

indicators.note: barking mad means crazy, so the letters are thrown into wild disorder

parts.note: the fourteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has left our English town, namely Barking in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a real town in east London, which disguises it as a place name; it is the British slang for crazy, as in barking mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Departed is a euphemism for dead, and the phrase is a similarly gentle way of saying someone has died.

clue.text: This is only fair

definitions.meaning: first meaning: merely, as in 'only a minute'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like someone insisting something is merely reasonable; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means merely as an adverb and equitable or right as an adjective, as in a decision handed down by a judge.

clue.text: Piece written in English — a line of letters

indicators.note: words written in a space sit inside it, enclosed by what surrounds them

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
piece is slang for a handgun
taken as written
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Describes a composition written in English that is just a single line of correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' suggests a piece of writing, but it is the gangster slang for a gun. The gun sits between the E and the A, then a railway line follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Epistolary means relating to or written in the form of correspondence, from the Greek word for a missive.

clue.text: Profanity in group accompanying one — right to be heard

indicators.note: being within something means it surrounds you on both sides

parts.note: a lot is a set or batch of things
and means together with
the Roman numeral for one
a cuss is a swear word

explanation.surface: Someone in a group is swearing, demanding their right to be heard.
explanation.walkthrough: The swear word sits inside the word for a group, then 'accompanying' and 'one' follow. The answer is a Latin legal term.
explanation.definitionFit: Locus standi is the legal standing a party needs before a court will hear its case.

clue.text: After routine work, a nervous condition

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed behind it in sequence

parts.note: a chore is a dull routine task
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone develops a nervous condition after too much routine work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a nervous condition' looks like the whole definition, but the 'a' is part of the wordplay, placed after the routine task.
explanation.definitionFit: Chorea is a neurological disorder causing involuntary jerky movements, as in Huntington's disease or St Vitus's dance.

clue.text: Such a blow shouldn't damage German school

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for German
Lancing College is an English boarding school in West Sussex

explanation.surface: A mild blow ought not to harm a German school.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancing College is a well-known private boarding school in West Sussex, on the English south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A glancing blow strikes at an angle and slides off, so it does little harm.

clue.text: Took time to go through lily garden

indicators.note: going through something means passing inside it, so it surrounds the traveller

parts.note: the arum is a lily, also called cuckoo pint
bore is the past tense of bear, to take or carry
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone takes their time wandering through a lily garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took time' reads as dawdling, but splits into the past of 'bear' and the abbreviation for time, which go inside the lily.
explanation.definitionFit: An arboretum is a botanical garden devoted to growing trees and shrubs for study and display.

clue.text: Girl having row with one Argentinian president

parts.note: an informal word for a girl
a tier is a row, as of seats
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A girl quarrels with one of Argentina's presidents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' suggests a quarrel, but here it is a line, as of seats. Leopoldo Galtieri led Argentina's junta during the 1982 Falklands War.
explanation.definitionFit: Leopoldo Galtieri was the military ruler and president of Argentina who ordered the 1982 invasion of the Falklands.

clue.text: Typical hail storm

parts.note: ave is the Latin greeting, as in Ave Maria
to storm is to rage

explanation.surface: A hailstorm of the ordinary, everyday kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hail storm' reads as weather, but 'hail' is a greeting and 'storm' a verb for fury.
explanation.definitionFit: Average describes what is normal or ordinary, the usual standard of a group.

clue.text: Broken leg reduced activity

indicators.note: something reduced has been cut down, losing its final part

parts.note: bust means broken
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A broken leg has limited someone's activity.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an injured person slowed down, while 'reduced' is the signal to cut the last letter off 'leg'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bustle is busy, energetic movement and commotion, the hum of people doing things.

clue.text: Plastic model turned into invention

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it

parts.note: a lie is a made-up story

indicators.note: turning something around makes it face the other way, back to front

parts.note: Kate Moss is a famous model

explanation.surface: A plastic model has been made into a new invention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' looks like a material, but it means bendy and supple. The model is the supermodel Kate Moss.
explanation.definitionFit: Plastic in its sense of pliable and flexible matches lissome, meaning supple and graceful in body.

clue.text: Silly cuts render film pathetic

definitions.note: a noun phrase read as 'pathetic film', with pathetic in its sense of arousing pity

indicators.note: cutting into something splits it apart so another part sits in the gap

parts.note: one who rends, tearing things apart
a jerk is a silly, foolish person

explanation.surface: Foolish edits make a movie feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'render' looks like the verb 'make', but it is one who rends. 'pathetic' is used in its old sense of moving to pity, not feeble.
explanation.definitionFit: A tear-jerker is a sentimental movie designed to make audiences cry, one full of pathos.

clue.text: Charlie featured in story about celebrity

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the word faces backwards
something featured in a work appears within it

parts.note: a tale is a story
C is Charlie in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone named Charlie appears in a story about a famous person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reads as 'concerning', but it turns the story round before Charlie is placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Éclat means brilliant success or renown, so it is a synonym for fame and acclaim.

clue.text: Undertaking convict's last request

indicators.note: the last of something is its final element, the end letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word
to ask is to request

explanation.surface: A prisoner on death row makes a final wish before execution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undertaking' brings undertakers and death to mind alongside a condemned man's last request, but it simply means a job.
explanation.definitionFit: An undertaking is a piece of work someone takes on, a job or assignment.

clue.text: A most serene death, using tissue

parts.note: taken as written
chill means relaxed, so the superlative is the calmest
death is the end of life
as in being on a medication, using it

explanation.surface: A peaceful passing achieved with the help of a handkerchief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tissue' suggests a paper hanky at a deathbed, but it is body tissue. 'Chillest' is modern slang for most relaxed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Achilles tendon is the band of fibrous connective material joining the calf muscles to the heel bone.

clue.text: The man's casual greetings

definitions.meaning: second meaning: more than one informal hello

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one person's relaxed hellos; the possessive and the plural greeting are two separate readings of the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive pronoun means belonging to a male person, and the plural of the informal salutation hi.

clue.text: Group is live with revolutionary online content

indicators.note: a revolution turns things right round, so the whole sequence runs backwards

parts.note: a set is a group
taken as written
to be is to exist or live
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A radical group goes live with material on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' looks like it describes a political group, but it turns the whole string of four pieces round.
explanation.definitionFit: Websites are pages hosted on the internet, which together make up the material people view on the web.

clue.text: First aid accepted by soldiers?

indicators.note: something accepted is taken in, so it ends up held inside

parts.note: soldiers are referred to as men
taken as written

explanation.surface: Troops receive first-aid treatment, with the question mark hinting at a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First aid' reads as one phrase, but 'First' is the definition and 'aid' the word that goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Maiden as an adjective means first of its kind, as in a maiden voyage or maiden speech.
